This page follows U.S. O*NET-SOC 27-1013.00, Fine Artists, Including Painters, Sculptors, and Illustrators (the fixed index gives this asset the Chinese name Artists, Painters; the text follows the official occupational scope). Fine-art work varies widely: easel painting and printmaking; sculpture and installation; commercial illustration and concept design; murals and public art; gallery representation and independent sales; and supplementing income through teaching and commissions. Before comparing roles or paths, check creative media and work scale, income sources (art sales, commissions, royalties, teaching, residency grants), gallery representation, credit and copyright terms, and material safety and venue rules.

Validate your judgment with a paper exercise: given a wholly fictional commission (theme and purpose, medium and size constraints, deadline and revision rounds, budget and materials list, credit and copyright terms), write the creative proposal and visual element arrangement, material and technique choices and reasons, schedule and revision milestones, portfolio and exhibition-promotion presentation, and cost and quotation breakdown. Identify terms requiring written client confirmation and matters governed by local copyright and material-safety rules.

Signals worth considering: willingness to maintain long-term creative practice and portfolio updates, accept unstable income and criticism, and actively submit to exhibitions and promote yourself. Signals calling for caution: relying only on inspiration without practice or organization, avoiding commission-term discussions, or treating one successful work as stable income.
This card is a career-exploration reference, not a hiring decision, ability score, artistic evaluation, or legal conclusion.

First consider whether you want to manage art-making as a long-term career: continuously practice techniques, maintain a portfolio, promote yourself, and handle commission and copyright terms. Validate this through this page's paper exercise and seven-day tasks.

Fine-art work cycles through conception, creation, finishing, presentation, and promotion. First research themes, trends, and references and form concepts. Then select media and techniques, prepare materials and tools, and arrange visual elements such as composition, color, and mass. Repeatedly test and adjust during creation, addressing material properties, drying and curing, structure, and durability. After completion, frame, mat, photograph, and catalog works. Then promote them through personal websites, catalogs, email, social platforms, and exhibition submissions, communicating with galleries, curators, clients, and collectors. Also accept illustration, portrait, mural, sculpture, and custom projects, deliver in contractual stages, and supplement income through teaching, residencies, or design services. Directions differ substantially: easel work emphasizes series and exhibition histories; commercial illustration emphasizes timely delivery and standardized files; public art and sculpture emphasize structure, installation, and safety approvals.

paragraphs: Work context | Fine-art work mostly occurs in individual, shared, or institutional studios, with substantial work in separate home studios. O*NET work-context data show predominantly irregular schedules (57%), with 43% regular; 68% work fewer than 40 hours per week and 26% work 40 hours (varying widely with self-employment and commissions). Work is mainly manual; 21% sit continually or almost continually and 16% about half the time. Precision and accuracy are relatively important (27% rate them important). Time pressure concentrates around delivery and installation milestones (strict deadlines daily for 29%, more than monthly for 31%, and more than yearly for 32%). Contact with others is constant for 29% and occurs about half the time for 16%. Email use is relatively infrequent (14% more than monthly, 13% never); 36% never encounter conflict situations. Primary subjects | Media and materials, sketches and studies, completed works, framing and matting materials, artwork records and photographs, costs and quotations, commission contracts, and exhibition applications. Collaboration | Galleries and curators, clients and commissioners, editors and authors, art directors, fellow artists and shared-studio partners, framers and shippers, and material suppliers. Tools and materials | Traditional painting and sculpture tools, printmaking and printing equipment, power and hand tools, computer-aided design and graphics software (such as Adobe Photoshop- and Illustrator-type tools), three-dimensional software and graphics tablets, and artwork cataloging and website tools. Governing rules | Material and venue safety requirements, chemical and solvent use and disposal rules, copyright and credit agreements, commission and sale contracts, and exhibition and public-art approval requirements. Records | Independently retain artwork records (medium, dimensions, year, photographs), materials and techniques, commissions and revisions, quotes and receipts, and exhibitions and sales. Practice boundaries | Artistic value judgments and market prices are not determined by the individual. Work includes researching themes, trends, and references to form concepts; integrating line, space, mass, color, and perspective to express ideas, emotions, or atmosphere; discussing content with clients, editors, authors, and art directors; completing works manually or digitally and handling material properties; framing, matting, photographing, and cataloging works; promoting through catalogs, email, websites, and exhibition submissions; accepting illustration, portrait, mural, sculpture, and custom projects; and potentially teaching techniques to children or adults.
entries.question: What do fine artists, including painters, sculptors, and illustrators, mainly do?

entries.answer: Responsibilities and outputs differ: this occupation centers on original artworks (paintings, sculptures, illustrations) credited to the creator. Craft artists emphasize practical or decorative handmade objects, craftsmanship, and materials; multimedia artists and animators emphasize digital media, animation, and interactive works; art directors coordinate project visual direction and teams rather than perform the main creation; commercial and industrial designers focus on functional and mass-production solutions for products and commercial systems; photographers focus on image capture and postproduction; graphic designers focus on commercial and informational visual communication.

entries.answer: O*NET places the occupation in Job Zone Three (medium preparation needed, SVP 6.0 to <7.0). Work mainly occurs in individual, shared, or separate home studios. Schedules are predominantly irregular (57%); 68% work fewer than 40 hours per week and 26% work 40 hours; 21% sit continually or almost continually and 16% about half the time. Precision and accuracy are rated important by 27%. Strict deadlines occur daily for 29%, more than monthly for 31%, and more than yearly for 32%; 29% have constant contact with others. Income and creative cycles fluctuate substantially; most practitioners need combined income sources. Education-category percentages were not obtained from the O*NET summary/detailed pages checked (insufficient evidence); this page does not substitute values.

entries.answer: This page suggests trialing reference organization, sketch candidates, layout trials, and artwork-record drafts as assistance areas, while responsible people review conception, media control, finishing, and credit. This is editorial analysis. ILO global potential-exposure research is not occupational adoption or job-outcome evidence, and O*NET tasks cannot establish that the entire occupation will not be replaced.

entries.answer: The exact occupation's 2025 median hourly wage was $26.68 and median annual wage $55,490; the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentiles were approximately $31,630, $37,560, $83,200, and $144,210/year (May 2025 OEWS, presented through O*NET). BLS OOH separately gives the craft and fine artists group median of $55,290, with the lowest 10% below $31,490 and highest 10% above $131,810, and group industry median annual wages: motion picture and sound recording $132,950; federal government excluding postal service $115,150; independent artists, writers, and performers $49,100; personal care services $38,790. The median is the midpoint of employee wage distribution, not starting pay. OEWS generally excludes self-employed people and artwork sales income; BLS also notes wide income variation among self-employed artists.

entries.answer: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Three. Its current education section lists some college without a degree, bachelor's, and high school categories for some roles; this page has not obtained category percentages and substitutes none. BLS OOH occupational-group typical entry preparation is a bachelor's degree, no related work experience, and long-term on-the-job training. This is U.S. group-level preparation, not a mandatory condition for every employer. Check Chinese qualifications, education, and artwork requirements against original target recruitment or project texts; this page has not obtained uniform national requirements.
entries.question: What education and qualifications are required?

entries.answer: O*NET lists no mandatory nationwide license for this occupation. Education, teaching credentials, and eligibility for established institutional posts depend on direction and organization type, such as school and university teaching roles, public-art project qualification and safety requirements, and some institutions' education thresholds. Verify these against original target-organization requirements, commission contracts, and local rules. This page provides no legal or compliance advice and does not equate certificates with creative ability.
entries.question: What certificates or licenses are needed?

entries.answer: Creators personally bear responsibility for quality, delivery, and credit; artistic value judgments and market prices are not determined by the individual. Professional institutions or competent authorities must confirm contracts, copyright, taxes, material safety, and public-art approvals. When using generative tools, tool output cannot serve as a deliverable artwork; check material sources and authorization item by item, and do not share client materials or unpublished works externally or use them for training. This page does not replace material safety and chemical-use requirements, copyright and credit rules, commission and sale contract requirements, or exhibition and public-art approval procedures, nor provide legal, tax, or safe-operating advice.
entries.question: Where are the responsibilities and boundaries of this work?

entries.answer: The exact occupation employed about 26,500 in 2024, with projected 2024—2034 decline (-1% or lower) and about 2,200 annual openings. Changes in art sales and commission markets fall outside this scope; personal income depends more on channels and artwork circulation. Common transitions include craft artists (need craftsmanship and material-production skills), multimedia artists and animators (digital painting and three-dimensional tools), art directors (visual coordination and team management), commercial and industrial designers (product functions and mass-production constraints), photographers (shooting and postproduction), graphic designers (graphic visuals and communication standards), agents and business managers of artists and performers (representation and business negotiation), and postsecondary art, drama, and music teachers (course design and teaching). Feasibility depends on target postings and local rules.

subject.summary: Create original artworks using varied media and techniques: work with materials such as pens, ink, watercolors, oils, clay, stone, wood, and metal, as well as software and graphics tablets; combine visual elements including line, space, mass, color, and perspective to express ideas, emotions, or atmosphere; discuss artwork nature and content with clients, editors, authors, and art directors; maintain portfolios demonstrating style and ability; promote work through catalogs, email, and personal websites and submit to exhibitions and galleries; keep learning techniques, following art-world developments, and researching topics; frame, mat, and install works, collaborating with engineers or technicians on large or installation works when needed; and potentially accept illustration, portrait, mural, sculpture, and custom commissions and teach art techniques to children or adults.
